entries.title: A perfect start to the day in Tamesha McGuire's kindergarten
entries.summary: A kindergarten teacher in Brooklyn opens the day with clear directions and calm routines. A good model of What To Do instructions with very young students.
entries.subject: Across subjects

entries.title: Jaime Johnson's formative writing routine
entries.summary: A middle school classroom video of students writing briefly and often in response to rich content, with an explanation of why short formative writing is worth making routine.
entries.subject: Literacy and English

entries.title: Details of the Turn and Task with Denarius Frazier
entries.summary: A variation on Turn and Talk in which pairs complete a maths task together rather than discuss a question, with notes on the details that make it productive.
entries.subject: Maths

entries.title: Explicit instruction in English
entries.summary: An AERO video on explicit instruction in English lessons. One of AERO's subject-specific practice videos.
entries.subject: Literacy and English

entries.title: Spacing and retrieval at Alfred Deakin High School
entries.summary: An AERO school example video on spacing and retrieval at Alfred Deakin High School. One of several AERO videos filmed in Australian schools.
entries.subject: Across subjects

entries.title: Using a staged approach to implementation
entries.summary: Second of five AERO explainers. Sets out the stages a school moves through when adopting an evidence-based practice, so leaders can judge where they are and plan next steps.

entries.title: Addressing enablers and barriers to implementation
entries.summary: Third of five AERO explainers. Shows leaders how to identify the local conditions that will help or hinder a new practice, and why to deal with them early.

entries.title: Using implementation strategies
entries.summary: Fourth of five AERO explainers. Helps leadership teams choose and prioritise the actions that support staff to take up a practice, matched to their own barriers and enablers.

entries.title: Monitoring implementation outcomes
entries.summary: Fifth of five AERO explainers. Describes which implementation outcomes to track, how to gather the data, and how to use it to check a practice is being used well.

entries.title: Evidence-informed implementation in schools
entries.summary: AERO discussion paper explaining why implementation matters and how its deliberate, structured approach was developed and refined with schools and regional teams. Comes with an A3 summary.

entries.title: The Maths Guarantee: A guide for principals
entries.summary: Companion to the Maths Guarantee report, written for primary principals. Describes what strong whole-school maths teaching involves and the steps leaders can take to build it.

entries.title: Student diversity: Supporting students through reasonable adjustments
entries.summary: A short Queensland Curriculum and Assessment Authority video on supporting students through reasonable adjustments. A handy opener for a staff conversation about what an adjustment is.
entries.subject: Across subjects

entries.title: Introduction to a multi-tiered system of supports
entries.summary: AERO's explainer sets out the features of a multi-tiered system of supports and what each tier involves, from strong classroom teaching to intensive help. Written for Years 7 to 9 but useful to any school.
entries.subject: Across subjects

entries.title: Supporting students significantly behind in literacy and numeracy
entries.summary: An AERO review of reviews on helping Years 7 to 9 students who are well behind in literacy and numeracy. It finds good grounds for multi-tiered support and looks at screening, progress monitoring and interventions.

entries.title: Learning difficulties: Victorian Department of Education overview and information guides
entries.summary: The Victorian department's overview of learning difficulties for teachers, covering possible signs, whole-school approaches, and links to its information guides on literacy difficulties, including dyslexia and dysgraphia, and numeracy difficulties, including dyscalculia.
entries.subject: Across subjects

entries.title: SPELD Victoria: Information for teachers
entries.summary: SPELD Victoria explains how a specific learning disorder differs from broader learning difficulties, why the impact on learning matters most, and what support the organisation offers Victorian teachers and schools.
entries.subject: Across subjects

entries.title: Understanding learning difficulties: The online guide for parents
entries.summary: A free online guide from AUSPELD that gives parents and carers current information about learning disabilities in children. Worth knowing so you can point families to something trustworthy.

entries.title: Special Educational Needs in Mainstream Schools: guidance report
entries.summary: The Education Endowment Foundation's guidance report gives five evidence-based recommendations for supporting pupils with additional needs in mainstream classrooms, with high quality everyday teaching at the centre.
entries.subject: Across subjects

entries.title: Assisting Students Struggling with Reading: Response to Intervention and Multi-Tier Intervention in the Primary Grades
entries.summary: A What Works Clearinghouse practice guide with five recommendations for finding struggling readers early and giving them tiered, evidence-based support in the primary years.

entries.title: You can't see DLD: An introduction to developmental language disorder
entries.summary: RADLD's short introduction to developmental language disorder, a common condition that is easy to miss. A good first video to show a whole staff.
entries.subject: Across subjects

entries.title: Developmental language disorder (DLD): The consensus explained
entries.summary: A short RADLD video explaining the consensus behind the term developmental language disorder. Helpful if older reports at your school still use other labels.
entries.subject: Across subjects

entries.title: The Hidden Disorder: Understanding developmental language disorder (full film)
entries.summary: RADLD's longer film on understanding developmental language disorder. Suits a staff meeting when you want more depth than a five-minute explainer.
entries.subject: Across subjects

entries.title: The challenge of rich vocabulary instruction for children with developmental language disorder
entries.summary: A short video from Australia's DLD Project on why rich vocabulary teaching is hard for children with developmental language disorder. Relevant to anyone planning vocabulary lessons.
entries.subject: Literacy and English

entries.title: DLD fact sheet
entries.summary: RADLD's fact sheet on developmental language disorder, from the international group that raises awareness of the condition. A short page to share with colleagues and families.

entries.title: CATALISE: A multinational and multidisciplinary Delphi consensus study. Identifying language impairments in children
entries.by: Bishop, Snowling, Thompson, Greenhalgh and the CATALISE consortium
entries.summary: The open-access consensus study in which an international expert panel worked towards agreed criteria for identifying children's language difficulties. It underpins the shift to the term developmental language disorder.

entries.title: School and DLD
entries.by: The Talking DLD Podcast (The DLD Project)
entries.summary: An episode of the Australian Talking DLD Podcast about school for children with developmental language disorder, and what it is like to watch a child struggle there.

entries.title: Phonics and DLD
entries.by: The Talking DLD Podcast (The DLD Project)
entries.summary: This Talking DLD Podcast episode explains why children with developmental language disorder are at higher risk of reading and spelling difficulty, and shares phonics strategies that help.

entries.title: What is dyslexia? Dyslexia explained
entries.summary: A short explainer from Understood on what dyslexia is. Brief enough to share with new staff, education support staff or families.
entries.subject: Literacy and English

entries.title: Definition of dyslexia
entries.summary: The International Dyslexia Association's current definition, adopted in October 2025. It describes dyslexia as difficulty with accurate or fluent word reading and spelling that sits on a continuum and persists despite effective teaching.
entries.subject: Literacy and English

entries.title: Defining and understanding dyslexia: Past, present and future
entries.summary: An open-access review that describes dyslexia as a difficulty in learning to decode and spell, places it among the neurodevelopmental disorders, and traces how understanding of it has changed.

entries.title: Providing Reading Interventions for Students in Grades 4 to 9
entries.summary: A What Works Clearinghouse practice guide on reading interventions for students in the upper primary and lower secondary years. One for leaders planning support for older struggling readers.

entries.title: What is dysgraphia in kids?
entries.summary: A two-minute explainer from Understood on what dysgraphia is in children. A simple starting point for staff and families.
entries.subject: Literacy and English

entries.title: What is dysgraphia?
entries.summary: Understood's article describes dysgraphia as a writing challenge that affects skills such as handwriting, typing and spelling, and explains how it can affect learning.
entries.subject: Literacy and English

entries.title: Teaching Elementary School Students to Be Effective Writers
entries.summary: A What Works Clearinghouse practice guide with four recommendations for improving primary students' writing, each with steps for putting it in place and answers to common obstacles.

entries.title: Facts and myths about dyscalculia
entries.summary: A short video from the Centre for Educational Neuroscience on facts and myths about dyscalculia. A sensible first watch before a staff discussion.
entries.subject: Maths

entries.title: What is dyscalculia?
entries.by: Numerical Cognition Laboratory, Western University, with Daniel Ansari
entries.summary: Professor Daniel Ansari of Western University explains what developmental dyscalculia is in five minutes. A good first watch before his longer webinar.
entries.subject: Maths

entries.title: Understanding dyscalculia
entries.summary: Dyscalculia specialist Cat Eadle explains what dyscalculia is, how it differs from other maths difficulties, and how mastery-style teaching can help. A short listen of a little over twenty minutes.

entries.title: Learning Difficulties Information Guide: Numeracy
entries.summary: Victoria's guide for teachers on numeracy difficulties, including dyscalculia. It explains core number abilities, a three-phase assessment process and intervention across the response to intervention tiers.
entries.subject: Maths

entries.title: Principles for designing intervention in mathematics
entries.summary: A short guide from the National Center on Intensive Intervention explaining key practices to use when teaching students who need intensive maths intervention.
entries.subject: Maths

entries.title: Supporting working memory in the primary classroom
entries.summary: A three-minute Education Endowment Foundation video on supporting working memory in the primary classroom. Short enough to watch and discuss in a team meeting.
entries.subject: Across subjects

entries.title: Understanding working memory: A classroom guide
entries.by: Susan Gathercole and Tracy Packiam Alloway
entries.summary: A classroom guide to working memory by researchers Susan Gathercole and Tracy Packiam Alloway, hosted by the University of Cambridge. Older, but still a well-known introduction for teachers.

entries.title: Developmental coordination disorder
entries.summary: A five-minute introduction to developmental coordination disorder from Ireland's National Council for Special Education. A quick primer for classroom teachers.
entries.subject: Across subjects

entries.title: ADHD factsheet for educators
entries.summary: A short fact sheet from the body behind Australia's ADHD clinical guideline. It explains why educators need to recognise possible ADHD and support students from preschool onwards.
entries.subject: Across subjects

entries.title: Educational adjustments for students with ADHD
entries.summary: Examples of common reasonable adjustments for students with ADHD, tied to the Disability Standards for Education. It also notes when anxiety or autism alongside ADHD may call for more.
entries.subject: Across subjects

entries.title: Australian Evidence-Based Clinical Practice Guideline for Attention Deficit Hyperactivity Disorder (ADHD)
entries.summary: The national guideline for identifying, diagnosing and supporting people with ADHD, approved by the NHMRC. Written for clinicians, and worth knowing as the reference point behind advice schools receive.

entries.title: Primary school teacher strategies for ADHD
entries.summary: A plain guide for primary teachers covering what ADHD is, the strengths these students bring, evidence-based strategies, best practice tips and points to consider across the curriculum.
entries.subject: Across subjects

entries.title: Attention deficit hyperactivity disorder (ADHD): Advice for school and home
entries.summary: The Royal Children's Hospital's fact sheet for families on supporting a child with ADHD at school and at home. Handy to share with parents so everyone is working from the same advice.
entries.subject: Across subjects

entries.title: What teachers can teach us about ADHD inclusion
entries.by: Flynn Vamos and Melanie Porter, for ADHD Australia
entries.summary: Two psychology researchers report what Australian primary teachers told them about including students with ADHD, which teachers described as the blind spot of inclusion.
entries.subject: Across subjects

entries.title: Supporting autistic and gender-diverse students at school
entries.by: Yellow Ladybugs, with the Department of Education, Victoria
entries.summary: A website guide to supporting autistic girls and gender-diverse students, covering masking, hidden anxiety, peer relationships, group work, executive functioning and class rules.
entries.subject: Across subjects

entries.title: Use visual schedules: Teaching practice
entries.summary: A step-by-step practice guide with classroom video on using visual schedules so students know what is coming, move between tasks smoothly and need fewer verbal prompts.
entries.subject: Across subjects

entries.title: Meet students' sensory needs: Teaching practice
entries.summary: A practice guide with video on getting to know students' sensory preferences and adjusting the room so they can stay comfortable, focused and safe.
entries.subject: Across subjects

entries.title: Transitions at Echuca College: Supporting autistic students with transition
entries.summary: A Victorian case study with short videos showing how Echuca College built a transition program with its feeder primary schools so new Year 7 students, including autistic students, start well.
entries.subject: Across subjects

entries.title: For primary teachers: Supporting autistic students' transition to secondary school
entries.summary: Amaze's tip sheet for Year 6 teachers on writing a transition plan with the student, the family and the secondary school before an autistic student moves on.
entries.subject: Across subjects

entries.title: Supporting autistic students: Diverse Learners Hub
entries.summary: The Victorian department's collection of guidance for schools on autistic students, linking to the Autism Education Strategy, transition tip sheets, behaviour support tools and partner organisations.
entries.subject: Across subjects

entries.title: Primary school teacher strategies for autism
entries.summary: A guide for primary teachers that sets out what autism is, the strengths autistic students bring, evidence-based strategies, best practice tips and curriculum considerations.
entries.subject: Across subjects

entries.title: Making best use of teaching assistants: Guidance report
entries.summary: Seven recommendations to help principals and leadership teams in primary and secondary schools make the best use of teaching assistants. The full report and a one-page poster are free to download.

entries.title: High quality teaching: The 'five-a-day' principle
entries.summary: A two-minute Education Endowment Foundation explainer of its 'five-a-day' principle, a set of five core practices that help all pupils succeed, including those with special educational needs. A quick opener for a staff meeting on Tier 1 teaching.
entries.subject: Across subjects

entries.title: Disability Standards: An introduction for educators
entries.summary: An introduction to the Disability Discrimination Act and the Disability Standards for Education, written with education law expert Professor Elizabeth Dickson. Covers educators' obligations, discrimination, harassment and victimisation.
entries.subject: Across subjects

entries.title: Disability Standards for Education: Resources for teachers and leaders
entries.summary: AITSL's collection of elaborations and videos showing how the Disability Standards for Education connect to the Teacher Standards and what they ask of teachers and leaders.
entries.subject: Across subjects

entries.title: Disability Standards for Education 2005
entries.summary: The Australian Government's home for the Standards, with fact sheets, exemplars of practice and the national guide to planning personalised learning and support.
entries.subject: Across subjects

entries.title: Individual Education Plans (IEPs): Victorian policy and guidance
entries.summary: The Victorian government school policy on Individual Education Plans. It sets out which students must have one, reminds schools of their duty to make reasonable adjustments, and links to guidance and templates.
entries.subject: Across subjects

entries.title: Student Support Groups: Victorian policy and guidance
entries.summary: The Victorian policy on Student Support Groups, the meeting of school, family and others that plans support for a student with disability or diverse learning needs.
entries.subject: Across subjects

entries.title: The Simple View of Reading: An explainer for teachers
entries.by: Linda Farrell, Michael Hunter, Marcia Davidson and Tina Osenga, Reading Rockets
entries.summary: A plain explanation of the model, in which reading comprehension depends on both decoding and language comprehension. It shows how to work out which of the two is holding a student back.

entries.title: Professional learning pathway: What is the Simple View of Reading and what does it mean for teaching?
entries.summary: Ready-made slides for leading a staff session on the Simple View of Reading, with the research explained, discussion questions, videos of model lessons and classroom resources.

entries.title: Scarborough's Reading Rope
entries.summary: Introduces Hollis Scarborough's 2001 Reading Rope, showing how the word recognition and language comprehension strands combine in skilled reading, and how teachers can use it to find where a reader is stuck.

entries.title: Updating the Language (and Literacy) House
entries.summary: Pamela Snow walks through her Language House on her blog, from the solid ground of early relationships up to the roof. She welcomes teachers using the model with attribution.

entries.title: The Writing Rope: The strands that are woven into skilled writing
entries.summary: Joan Sedita's own article introducing the Writing Rope, which sorts the skills of writing into five strands, namely critical thinking, syntax, text structure, writing craft and transcription.
entries.strand: The Writing Rope and views of writing

entries.title: Understanding the reading process
entries.by: Deslea Konza, for the South Australian Department of Education and Children's Services
entries.summary: A short, readable paper that pulls the big reading reviews into six components, from oral language and phonological awareness through to fluency and comprehension. Good pre-reading for a staff meeting.
entries.strand: The Big Six and the five components

entries.title: Introduction to the science of reading
entries.summary: AERO's overview of how children learn to read. It introduces the Simple View of Reading, Scarborough's Reading Rope and the core reading skills, and explains why explicit, systematic teaching matters.

entries.title: Science of Reading: The Defining Guide
entries.summary: The Reading League's guide to what the science of reading is and what it is not. The free eBook is a helpful shared reference when the term is being used loosely.

entries.title: Teaching Reading Is Rocket Science: What expert teachers of reading should know and be able to do
entries.summary: Louisa Moats on what expert teachers of reading should know and be able to do, in the 2020 edition of her paper for American Educator.

entries.title: Structured literacy: Effective instruction for students with dyslexia and related reading difficulties
entries.summary: The International Dyslexia Association explains structured literacy, covering what is taught, from phonemes to sentence structure and meaning, and how it is taught, explicitly, systematically and cumulatively.

entries.title: How Knowledge Helps: It speeds and strengthens reading comprehension, learning and thinking
entries.summary: Daniel Willingham explains why knowledge is more than grist for the mill, and how what students already know speeds and strengthens their reading comprehension, learning and thinking.

entries.title: Rethinking How to Promote Reading Comprehension
entries.summary: Hugh Catts argues that reading comprehension is not a single skill that can be taught and tested on its own, because it depends on the reader's knowledge, the text and the purpose for reading.

entries.title: Oral language (Understanding the reading process, paper 1.1)
entries.by: Deslea Konza, for the South Australian Department of Education and Children's Services
entries.summary: Deslea Konza explains how oral language shapes later reading, with classroom strategies such as wait time, simpler teacher talk, think-alouds, shared story books and daily table talk.

entries.title: How Spelling Supports Reading: And why it is more regular and predictable than you may think
entries.summary: Louisa Moats on how spelling supports reading, and why English spelling is more regular and predictable than many people think. The article downloads as a PDF from this page.

entries.title: How Words Cast Their Spell: Spelling is an integral part of learning the language, not a matter of memorization
entries.by: Malatesha Joshi, Rebecca Treiman, Suzanne Carreker and Louisa Moats, American Educator
entries.summary: Four researchers make the case that spelling is an integral part of learning the language and not a matter of memorising. The article downloads as a PDF from this page.

entries.title: The Science of Reading Progresses: Communicating advances beyond the Simple View of Reading
entries.summary: The paper that proposed the Active View of Reading. Duke and Cartwright set out three advances since the Simple View, including the overlap between word recognition and language comprehension and the part played by active self-regulation.

entries.title: SOLAR: The Science of Language and Reading
entries.summary: Pamela Snow's paper proposing the Science of Language and Reading framework, which places oral language at the centre of learning to read. It sets out her Language House in full.

entries.title: Teaching Reading: Why the 'Fab Five' should be the 'Big Six'
entries.summary: Deslea Konza's case for adding oral language and early literacy experiences to the National Reading Panel's five elements, which gives the Big Six.
entries.strand: The Big Six and the five components

entries.title: Report of the National Reading Panel: Teaching children to read
entries.summary: The summary report of the United States National Reading Panel, the review behind the five components of phonemic awareness, phonics, fluency, vocabulary and comprehension.
entries.strand: The Big Six and the five components

entries.title: Teaching Reading: Report and recommendations (National Inquiry into the Teaching of Literacy)
entries.by: Ken Rowe and the National Inquiry into the Teaching of Literacy
entries.summary: The report of Australia's 2005 national inquiry, which reviewed the research on teaching literacy and how well new teachers were being prepared to teach reading.

entries.title: Independent review of the teaching of early reading: Final report (the Rose Review)
entries.by: Jim Rose, for the Department for Education and Skills
entries.summary: Jim Rose's 2006 review of the teaching of early reading for the Department for Education and Skills in England. Free to download from the Digital Education Resource Archive.

entries.title: How the Science of Reading Informs 21st-Century Education
entries.by: Petscher, Cabell, Catts, Compton, Foorman and colleagues
entries.summary: Twelve researchers from the Florida Center for Reading Research sort the claims made for the science of reading into those with compelling evidence, promising evidence and little evidence. Free on PubMed Central.

entries.title: The Role of Background Knowledge in Reading Comprehension: A critical review
entries.by: Reid Smith, Pamela Snow, Tanya Serry and Lorraine Hammond
entries.summary: An open-access critical review of the research on the part background knowledge plays in reading comprehension, published in Reading Psychology in 2021.

entries.title: Language is literacy is language: Positioning speech-language pathology in education policy, practice, paradigms and polemics
entries.summary: Pamela Snow's Elizabeth Usher Memorial Lecture, published as an open-access paper, on where speech-language pathology sits in education policy, practice and debate.

entries.title: The Simple View of Reading and its extension as the Cognitive Foundations Framework: A conversation with Dr Wesley Hoover
entries.summary: Wesley Hoover talks through the Simple View of Reading and how the Cognitive Foundations Framework extends it. The podcast is produced by a publisher, Voyager Sopris Learning.

entries.title: Hard Words: Why aren't kids being taught to read?
entries.summary: Emily Hanford's documentary on what research shows about how children learn to read, why many educators do not know that science, and how one Pennsylvania district set about changing its teaching.

entries.title: Sold a Story
entries.summary: Emily Hanford's investigative podcast on how children learn to read and why the research often does not reach classrooms. A second season looks beyond reading to teaching itself.

entries.title: Videos: See phoneme segmentation and blending in the classroom
entries.summary: Six short classroom clips, most from Atlanta schools. Teachers lead spoken blending and segmenting games, and a kindergarten teacher builds words with letters and blends the sounds to read them.
entries.subject: Literacy and English

entries.title: Video: See phoneme manipulation in the classroom
entries.summary: Ashley Powell, a first grade teacher in Oklahoma, works with a small group. Students touch a felt square for each sound, say the phonemes, then swap one sound to make a new word.
entries.subject: Literacy and English

entries.title: Should we do phoneme awareness activities without letters?
entries.summary: Weighs up the debate about oral-only phonemic awareness. The evidence favours using letters, though short spoken blending and segmenting games still have a place before school and in intervention.

entries.title: What the research says about phonemic awareness instruction
entries.summary: A short summary of the research, from the National Reading Panel's findings to the current advice that most children do best when phoneme awareness is taught with letters.

entries.title: Foundational Skills to Support Reading for Understanding in Kindergarten Through 3rd Grade
entries.summary: A practice guide with four recommendations for teaching early reading. The second is to develop awareness of the sounds in speech and how they link to letters, with steps for putting it into practice.

entries.title: Want to Improve Children's Writing? Don't Neglect Their Handwriting
entries.summary: Steve Graham explains why handwriting places the earliest limits on young writers, and how teaching it well improves the amount and quality of what children write, not only its legibility.

entries.title: Our research shows children produce better pieces of writing by hand. But they need keyboard skills too
entries.by: Anabela Malpique, Deborah Pino Pasternak and Susan Ledger, The Conversation
entries.summary: Researchers report that Year 2 students in Perth wrote longer, better stories by hand than on a laptop, and explain why handwriting and typing both need to be taught.

entries.title: Handwriting and letter formation: Skill explainer
entries.summary: A two-part guide to why handwriting is taught and how to teach letter formation explicitly, with the words to say while modelling each lower-case letter.

entries.title: Oracy floats on a sea of knowledge
entries.summary: Didau weighs England's push to give oracy equal status with reading and writing. He argues students speak well when they know a lot, and sets out what schools should prioritise instead.

entries.title: How to embed writing instruction into your English curriculum
entries.summary: Didau explains how a Years 7 to 9 English curriculum can teach sentence and paragraph skills in short, controlled bursts, delaying extended essays until the parts are secure. It also promotes his resource pack.

entries.title: My kingdom for a reliable curriculum review
entries.summary: Korbey looks at how US curriculum review platforms rate materials, why each one examines only part of the picture, and why evidence of impact is so often missing when schools choose.

entries.title: Great teaching is neither scripted nor improvised
entries.summary: Swain offers a simple matrix of preparation and deviation to show why expert teaching is neither rigid script-reading nor improvisation, and why responsive teaching depends on thorough preparation.

entries.title: Students can’t learn in cultures of perfectionism or opting out
entries.summary: Swain describes two classroom cultures that block learning, opting out and perfectionism, and explains how a deliberate culture of error and expected participation helps students take the risks learning needs.

entries.title: Explicit teaching isn’t regurgitation
entries.summary: Swain answers the claim that explicit teaching produces passive learners. He shows how building secure foundations first lets students generate and apply ideas, so knowledge becomes something to think with.

entries.title: School culture is something you cultivate
entries.summary: A follow-up on culture of error that turns to whole-school consistency. Swain discusses phasing in change, no opt out with support, and the difference between collaboration and mere co-operation among staff.

entries.title: Three big areas for development in teaching for 2026-7
entries.summary: From hundreds of lesson visits, Sherrington names three priorities for most schools, inclusive teaching, responsive teaching and teaching through talk, and links to his earlier writing on each.

entries.title: Powerful habit changes for more inclusive teaching
entries.summary: A practical list of small changes from Sherrington's training, including cold calling done well, structured think-pair-share, whole answers, show-me boards and rehearsal, all aimed at involving every student in thinking.

entries.title: Learning through talk
entries.summary: Sherrington uses a simple memory model to explain how talk supports learning, and argues that if talk helps students learn, routines must give every student the chance to talk, not just a few.

entries.title: Valuing every voice: the false premise that 'hands up' respondents are more worthy of being listened to
entries.summary: Sherrington explains why relying on hands up lets confident students dominate, and makes the case for routines that ensure every student's thinking is heard and explored.

entries.title: Oracy in practice: knowledge and the Voice 21 Benchmarks
entries.summary: Sherrington rejects the idea that oracy competes with knowledge, and shows how the Voice 21 benchmarks place subject knowledge at the centre of talk in a rich curriculum.

entries.title: Oracy in practice: creating an oracy-rich curriculum by harnessing everyday routines
entries.summary: Using his tree metaphor, Sherrington sets out how a school can build an oracy-rich curriculum from routines teachers already use, starting with shared values about talk and listening.

entries.title: The flow of ideas on the road to sustained, nuanced impact
entries.summary: Sherrington describes a predictable pattern when ideas such as retrieval practice spread, from scattered pockets to mass adoption that loses nuance, then to deeper, better practice, and why leaders should expect it.

entries.title: Reading Comprehension Is Not a Skill
entries.summary: Drawing on new research and his own teaching, Hendrick argues that comprehension depends far more on knowing word meanings than on generic strategies, and makes the case for rich vocabulary teaching as an equity lever.

entries.title: 10 Rules for Designing Effective Learning
entries.summary: Hendrick distils Engelmann and Carnine's Theory of Instruction into ten design rules about examples, boundaries and sequencing, showing how careful instructional design helps every student form concepts, not only the strongest.

entries.title: Defending the Science of Learning
entries.summary: Hendrick answers common criticisms of the science of learning, such as claims it is dogma or de-skills teachers, and sets out the research base and the equity case for it.

entries.title: Privileging the Already Privileged
entries.summary: Hendrick argues that minimally guided discovery learning shifts the work onto students and favours those who arrive with advantages, making explicit instructional design the more progressive and equitable choice.

entries.title: Why You Cannot Believe Your Way Into Learning
entries.summary: Hendrick reviews new evidence that growth mindset interventions do little for achievement on their own, and argues that real success through effective practice is what builds students' belief in themselves.

entries.title: The untold story of Bloom's Taxonomy and the pyramid that never was
entries.summary: A history of how a 1956 handbook for classifying exam questions became a pyramid that ranks thinking above knowledge, and why that reading misleads curriculum and lesson planning.

entries.title: Rethinking Retrieval Practice: Remembering Is Not Knowing
entries.summary: Using two recent studies, Hendrick shows that students can remember more yet apply no better, and argues retrieval practice works best to maintain knowledge that has first been properly understood.

entries.title: The Lethal Mutation of Retrieval Practice
entries.summary: Hendrick sets out five ways retrieval practice goes wrong in classrooms, including quizzing on material never learnt and skipping spacing, and discusses a study on retrieval with complex material.

entries.title: We Need to Talk About Scaffolding
entries.summary: Hendrick examines a careful replication of the famous 1978 scaffolding study that found no benefit from the classic rule of more help after failure, and considers what this means for teaching and tutoring.

entries.title: In Search of Vygotsky
entries.summary: Hendrick traces how translations and selective readings turned Vygotsky into a champion of discovery learning, and argues his own work placed far more weight on teaching systematic, scientific concepts.

entries.title: Does Explicit Instruction Work For Students with Learning Difficulties?
entries.summary: Hendrick discusses a computational study suggesting students with ADHD and dyslexia face distinct extra costs in unguided learning, and why clear, explicit guidance matters even more for them.

entries.title: Is There a Science of Writing?
entries.summary: Hendrick asks why writing research, which is substantial, has had far less influence than the science of reading, and outlines what the evidence says about teaching writing.
entries.strand: The Writing Rope and views of writing

entries.title: Responsive Teaching Part 1: Learning is Recursive Not Linear
entries.summary: Written while working with Australian schools, Hendrick explains why learning is recursive rather than linear, what responsive teaching involves, and which lethal mutations to avoid.

entries.title: Orthographic Skeletons: Can Children Start Learning How Words Are Spelled Before They've Seen it in Print?
entries.summary: Hendrick explains research suggesting children form an early guess at a word's spelling from hearing it, which helps explain why oral vocabulary supports later reading and spelling.

entries.title: How to Make Social Studies "Magical"
entries.summary: Wexler visits a New York sixth-grade civics class where rapid, game-like recall of history facts gives students the knowledge to analyse ideas, showing memorisation and engagement can go together.

entries.title: A (Relatively) Easy Way to Boost Reading Comprehension
entries.summary: Wexler reports a study isolating complex syntax as a factor in comprehension, and describes how teachers can spot sentence-level difficulties and use sentence-level writing activities to teach them.

entries.title: Don't Forget to Elaborate
entries.summary: Wexler argues that explicit instruction and retrieval practice are not enough on their own, and that students also need to elaborate on new knowledge, with writing as a practical way to do it.

entries.title: How Can You Tell If a Curriculum Truly Builds Knowledge?
entries.summary: Using one widely adopted US program as a case study, Wexler explains how a curriculum can look knowledge-building but lack depth and coherence, and why ratings can mislead schools.

entries.title: Most Struggling Students Get "Incoherent" Instruction
entries.summary: Wexler contrasts a struggling reader whose interventions are unrelated to class work with one whose support reinforces the core curriculum, and argues that coherence across support lowers cognitive load.

entries.title: Do Knowledge-Building Curricula Really Lack Whole Books?
entries.summary: Wexler examines complaints that knowledge-building literacy curricula lack whole books, separating fair criticism from misunderstanding and noting what teachers report about students' stamina with longer texts.

entries.title: Many Students Struggle to Read Beyond Third Grade
entries.summary: Wexler explains why many older students still struggle to read, why upper-grade teachers need different training from early-years teachers, and which approaches look promising.

entries.title: The Writing Effect
entries.summary: Wexler reviews write-to-learn research, linking writing to retrieval and elaboration, and argues that writing would boost learning more reliably if teachers made it manageable through explicit sentence-level instruction.

entries.title: To Boost Learning, Weave Writing Activities Into Regular Instruction
entries.summary: Wexler shows how explicit writing activities can be woven into discussion of content-rich lessons, moving between talk and writing to deepen understanding and build stronger writers.

entries.title: What Do We Mean by "Reading Comprehension Instruction"?
entries.summary: Wexler untangles competing claims that schools teach too little or too much comprehension, tracing the debate back to Durkin and arguing that literacy and content teaching must work together.

entries.title: Uncovering the "Hidden Lives" of Learners
entries.summary: Wexler introduces Graham Nuthall's research on what students actually learn in class, including his finding that students typically need to meet a concept several times before it sticks.

entries.title: The Key to Motivating Students--and Maybe Everyone Else Too
entries.summary: Wexler argues that motivation tends to follow achievement, so clear teaching that lets students succeed is a more reliable way to motivate them than choice, relevance or rewards.

entries.title: Unpacking explicit teaching
entries.summary: Written as Australian governments fund evidence-informed reform, Ashman sets out a working definition of explicit teaching, how it works within a lesson and across a sequence, and which versions the evidence supports.

entries.title: Five arguments against explicit teaching, #1: rote memorisation versus deeper understanding
entries.summary: The first in a series preparing teachers for common objections. Ashman examines the claim that explicit teaching only builds rote recall, drawing on empirical evidence and theory about understanding.

entries.title: Five arguments against explicit teaching, #2: creativity and other higher order skills
entries.summary: Ashman tackles the claim that explicit teaching stifles creativity and higher-order thinking, tracing the idea to readings of Bloom's taxonomy and arguing for the whole explicit teaching process instead.

entries.title: Five arguments against explicit teaching, #3: explicit teaching kills teacher creativity and autonomy
entries.summary: Ashman takes on the claim that explicit teaching kills teacher creativity and autonomy, arguing that constraint can free creativity and that shared lesson plans leave room to refine one thing well.

entries.title: Five arguments against explicit teaching, #4: explicit teaching takes no account of student differences
entries.summary: Ashman responds to the objection that explicit teaching ignores individual differences, questioning differentiation as a cure-all and explaining which differences between students really matter for instruction.

entries.title: Five arguments against explicit teaching, #5: explicit teaching is demotivating
entries.summary: The last in Ashman's series takes on the claim that explicit teaching kills motivation, arguing from experience and research that early success through clear instruction is what motivates learners.

entries.title: Explicit teaching is inclusive
entries.summary: Ashman links tiered support to whole-class teaching, arguing that explicit teaching, including structured literacy, is a strong Tier 1 approach for learning and behaviour and is inclusive of students with disabilities.

entries.title: Is productive struggle ethical?
entries.summary: Ashman questions the popular idea, especially in maths, of designing lessons so students struggle first, examining the case for constructivism and productive failure and the ethics of deliberate difficulty.

entries.title: Boring lessons and what to do about them
entries.summary: A short, practical reflection on keeping whole-class explicit teaching lively, using voice, story, urgency and momentum, and why being interesting does not mean being an entertainer.

entries.title: Building Thinking Classrooms is still nonsense
entries.summary: Ashman critiques Building Thinking Classrooms, arguing that it defines explained and modelled instruction as not thinking and that its claims are not supported by cognitive science.

entries.title: Universal Design for Learning (UDL) is the new learning styles
entries.summary: Ashman discusses a paper drawing parallels between Universal Design for Learning and learning styles, and raises concerns about its evidence base, its planning workload and its spread into policy.

entries.title: Tip #49: Play the "Does that make sense?" game
entries.summary: A short classroom tip for breaking the habit of asking "Does that make sense?", which rarely reveals understanding, by turning it into a game and replacing it with better checks.

entries.title: Tip #47: "Can you get us started..."
entries.summary: Barton shows how rephrasing a cold-call question as an invitation to begin, rather than to give the one right answer, lowers the stakes and gets more reluctant students contributing.

entries.title: Tip #48: Check for listening to see if your explanation is clear and concise
entries.summary: Using two versions of a maths explanation, Barton shows how to plan explanations that are clear and free of clutter, and how checking students were listening reveals whether an explanation worked.

entries.title: Research Bite #56: Updated meta-analysis of the research on response cards
entries.summary: Barton summarises a meta-analysis of 29 studies finding that response cards, where every student answers at once, lift participation and quiz results and reduce off-task behaviour compared with hands up.

entries.title: Research Bite #53: Spacing and retrieval practice for mathematics learning
entries.summary: Barton breaks down a meta-analysis on spacing and retrieval practice in maths, including where spacing helps most and what the findings mean for planning practice and review in maths classrooms.

entries.title: Research Bite #61: A scoping review of 20 years of research on differentiation
entries.summary: Barton summarises Linda Graham and colleagues' review of differentiation research, which found the term used for very different, sometimes incompatible practices, and discusses what that means for teachers.

entries.title: Research Bite #68: Worked examples and self-explanation prompts and students' maths motivation
entries.summary: Barton unpacks a study of primary maths worksheets pairing correct and incorrect worked examples with self-explanation prompts, looking at their effect on students' motivation and how they view errors.

entries.title: Research Bite #73: Why peer discussion improves student performance on in-class concept questions
entries.summary: Barton explains a study testing whether students improve after discussing a concept question because they understand it or copy classmates, and what it suggests about using peer discussion in lessons.

entries.title: Research Bite #65: High maths anxiety and lower maths achievement across 90 countries
entries.summary: Barton summarises a very large international analysis linking maths anxiety with lower achievement, and considers what teachers can reasonably take from a correlational finding of this kind.

entries.title: Research Bite #79: When and how to use visuals effectively, a meta-analysis of dual coding
entries.summary: Barton breaks down a meta-analysis of classroom experiments on adding pictures and diagrams to explanations, including where visuals helped most and how to use them well.

entries.title: Research Bite #64: The Student Grouping Study
entries.summary: Barton summarises an EEF evaluation comparing setting and mixed-attainment groups in lower secondary maths, covering effects on progress and confidence and the implications for schools deciding how to group.

entries.title: What is Comparative Judgement and why does it work?
entries.summary: A clear introduction to comparative judgement, where teachers compare two pieces of writing rather than marking against a rubric, why it is more reliable, and what adding AI judges changes.

entries.title: Why grades are misleading
entries.summary: Christodoulou explains why grades suggest sharper differences between students than really exist, the distortions this causes, and why reporting the probability of each grade gives a more honest picture.

entries.title: How to write a good rubric (for humans and AI)
entries.summary: Drawing on a national history essay assessment, Christodoulou looks at what judges reward, including factual accuracy, and offers advice on writing clearer criteria for both human and AI markers.

entries.title: But my students like written comments
entries.summary: Christodoulou argues that detailed written comments describe weaknesses without helping students fix them, and makes the case for whole-class feedback and practice that changes what students do next.

entries.title: Why personalising education based on student interests doesn’t work
entries.summary: Christodoulou explains why tailoring lessons to students' interests rarely improves learning, and warns that arguments for personalisation often promise better pacing but deliver isolated screen time.

entries.title: What if transferable skills don’t exist?
entries.summary: Christodoulou revisits a myth from her own book, arguing that skills such as creativity and critical thinking depend on knowledge of a particular domain, and considers what follows for schools.

entries.title: Do knowledge-rich curriculums cause mental health problems?
entries.summary: Christodoulou tests the claim that England's knowledge-rich reforms worsened young people's mental health, comparing trends across the UK nations and concluding the evidence does not support the link.

entries.title: Are we living in a stupidogenic society?
entries.summary: Starting with her grandmother's mental arithmetic, Christodoulou asks whether technology lets us skip the practice that builds knowledge and skill, and why schools need to keep those cognitive muscles working.

entries.title: What is the point of learning to write in a world with AI?
entries.summary: Using a marathon metaphor, Christodoulou explains why students should still learn to write when AI can produce text, because the purpose of writing in school is the thinking it builds.

entries.title: Can we teach students to spot misinformation?
entries.summary: Christodoulou describes how many students fail to spot even obvious hoaxes online, and argues that background knowledge matters more than generic media literacy for judging what is true.

entries.title: What should we do about the "forgotten third"?
entries.summary: Christodoulou argues that the answer for older students who leave school without basic English and maths is better teaching of foundational skills, rather than steering them early into vocational routes.

entries.title: On explicit teaching and student behaviour
entries.summary: Drawing on her doctoral literature review, Birch sets out research linking explicit teaching with better student behaviour and other non-academic outcomes, and argues that academic success underpins wellbeing.

entries.title: On how to change your mind
entries.summary: Birch explains how new research on prior knowledge and the expertise reversal effect has partly changed her view on whether gifted learners always need explicit teaching before problem solving.

entries.title: On what we mean when we say "inclusive" teaching
entries.summary: Birch argues that inclusive teaching should build on the needs students share, such as clear explanation, predictability and guided practice, rather than treating a growing group of students as individual adjustments.

entries.title: On the transformative power of teaching first
entries.summary: Birch explains how the TAPPLE sequence from Explicit Direct Instruction changed her secondary English teaching, walking through each step and what it is not, including its effect on workload.

entries.title: On chasing the rainbow of intrinsic motivation
entries.summary: Birch questions the hunt for intrinsic motivation in school subjects and describes realistic alternatives, such as teacher enthusiasm, clear rationales and success, that support students' effort and learning.

entries.title: On the cycle of avoidance
entries.summary: Using her own fear of flying, Birch argues that school accommodations for anxiety can reinforce avoidance, and that participation and low-stakes testing better support students' competence and belonging.

entries.title: On how to make any teacher an expert in writing
entries.summary: Birch describes implementing a whole-school writing approach in a secondary school, including the tools used and how to support teachers who feel unsure about teaching writing in their subject.

entries.title: On powerful knowledge
entries.summary: Through a reading passage that leaves most readers lost, Birch shows how background knowledge shapes comprehension, and argues an ambitious curriculum is how schools give every student access to powerful knowledge.

entries.title: On the five big risks to reform
entries.summary: Birch welcomes Australia's shift towards explicit teaching but names five risks to the reform, including rushed rollout, thin resources and unclear messaging, and how leaders can avoid another pendulum swing.

entries.title: On cold calling
entries.summary: Birch makes the case for cold calling in secondary classrooms as a lever for equity, citing research that it increases voluntary participation, and offers advice on making it work well.

entries.title: On high quality instructional materials
entries.summary: Prompted by a Productivity Commission report, Birch discusses why quality-assured lesson materials matter for teacher time and student outcomes in Australia, and how they relate to teacher expertise.

entries.title: On reading spines
entries.summary: Birch reflects on co-creating a reading spine, a planned sequence of whole texts across the years, and on why schools should ensure every student has a copy of the books they study.

entries.title: The Beautiful (and Impossible) Dream of Transferable Reading Skills
entries.summary: In an excerpt from his guide to the science of reading, Lemov explains why the hope of teaching transferable comprehension skills is a chimera, and why inference and understanding depend on knowledge.

entries.title: Next Level Reading Lesson Design
entries.summary: Lemov shares highlights from a Year 3 teacher's unit on the novel Stone Fox, showing how shared reading, fluency, vocabulary and writing prompts are planned into lessons built around a whole text.

entries.title: Re-Centering the Text
entries.summary: Lemov explains the idea of re-centring the text, reading together in class from the same book, and why it builds attention, fluency and shared meaning when technology competes for students' focus.

entries.title: Two Small Secrets To (Cold Call) Success
entries.summary: Using a classroom video, Lemov highlights two small details that make cold calling smoother and more positive, including polling the class after a short writing task before calling on anyone.

entries.title: The Most Important Habit in Your Classroom is Easy to Overlook
entries.summary: Lemov shares a video of a teacher building the habit of following directions, and explains why such everyday routines are the hidden foundation for rich learning moments.

entries.title: “Norm Amplification,” psychological safety and academic rigor
entries.summary: Drawing on Peps Mccrea's work, Lemov explains how students' sense of what peers approve of shapes their behaviour, and how teachers can amplify positive norms, especially around academic effort.

entries.title: The Room Seemed to Ache with Loneliness: Jaime Johnson’s Formative Writing Routine
entries.summary: Through video of a middle school teacher, Lemov explains formative writing, where students write to discover what they think, and shows how to make it a regular routine in response to rich texts.

entries.title: How Jaime Johnson’s Shared Reading Leads to Vibrant Discussion
entries.summary: Lemov shows how shared oral reading of a whole book frees students' working memory for discussion, using classroom video to illustrate how reading together leads to richer conversation.

entries.title: Stories are cognitively (psychologically) privileged
entries.summary: Lemov shares notes on Daniel Willingham's explanation of why stories are easier to understand and remember, and what that means for how teachers structure explanations and use shared stories.

entries.title: George Bonanno's "The End of Trauma" and Notes on "Trauma" & "Trauma Informed"
entries.summary: Lemov recommends George Bonanno's research on resilience and cautions that loose use of the words trauma and trauma-informed in schools can lead to well-meant but counterproductive responses.

entries.title: The de-intellectualisation of teaching
entries.summary: Hughes argues that reducing teaching to a list of approved moves strips out the subject knowledge, judgement and responsiveness that make it intellectual work, and that pupils lose out when that happens.

entries.title: When cognitive science becomes a checklist: the problem with generic lesson structures
entries.summary: Hughes explains how well-meant whole-school lesson structures built from cognitive science can become rigid checklists, and why subject knowledge and teacher judgement must shape how principles are used.

entries.title: Wellbeing isn't cake in the staff room: it's professionalism done properly
entries.summary: Hughes argues that staff wellbeing comes less from treats and gestures than from manageable workloads, clear systems, purposeful professional development and a culture that takes teachers' growth seriously.

entries.title: Death by differentiation
entries.summary: Hughes contrasts differentiation that dumbs down tasks or multiplies planning with responsive teaching, which keeps the learning ambitious for everyone and adjusts support when evidence shows it is needed.

entries.title: From principle to practice: lessons I have learnt about implementing lesson principles well
entries.summary: Hughes reflects on a year implementing research-informed lesson principles across a trust, sharing what helps principles move from a published document to consistent, thoughtful practice in classrooms.

entries.title: To UDL or not to UDL? I have questions
entries.summary: Hughes questions how Universal Design for Learning is presented to teachers, raising concerns about workload, unlimited student choice and drift towards learning-styles thinking.

entries.title: 'Our kids can't': the soft bigotry of low expectations
entries.summary: Prompted by a Victorian primary principal's talk, Hughes examines how the phrase "our kids can't" lowers expectations, and how explicit, systematic teaching makes ambitious goals reachable for all students.

entries.title: Why I hate popsicle sticks for cold calling
entries.summary: Hughes explains why drawing names at random is not the same as purposeful cold calling, and how teachers can choose who to ask based on what they need to find out.

entries.title: Faded scaffolding: keeping challenge high while building independence
entries.summary: Hughes explains how scaffolds such as sentence starters and writing frames should be temporary and targeted, keeping tasks ambitious and gradually removed as students show they are ready.

entries.title: Deliberate practice: why great teaching isn't built on experience alone
entries.summary: Hughes explains why experience alone does not make teachers better, and how focused, repeated rehearsal of specific techniques within coaching helps teachers turn professional learning into classroom practice.

entries.title: Rehearsal Is More Than Role Play
entries.summary: Hughes argues that rehearsal in professional learning should not default to role play, and that coaches should ask what kind of practice best suits the particular part of teaching being developed.

entries.title: Why are we still leaving mentors to figure it out?
entries.summary: Comparing England and Australia, Hughes argues that strong teachers do not automatically make strong mentors, and that mentor training is a worthwhile investment in new teachers and retention.

entries.title: Ten Lethal Mutations of Educational Research
entries.summary: Hughes names ten ways research gets distorted on its way into schools, such as slogans and rigid rules, and suggests how leaders can keep the nuance of the original evidence.

entries.title: "Completed it, mate": teacher identity and Australia's reading wars
entries.summary: Hughes reflects on the hostility in Australia's debates about explicit teaching and the science of reading, linking it to teacher identity and suggesting how leaders can help teachers reconsider practice.

entries.title: In conversation about handwriting
meta: with Shannan Salvestro and Vanessa Hewitt
entries.summary: Two members of the NSW Department of Education's literacy team discuss why handwriting matters so much and how to teach it effectively. About 23 minutes, with a transcript.
